sections.text: Below is the shortest high-confidence triage list I can justify from the record. I would **start with WS-POL-E, then WS-POL-F+G, then WS-POL-L / H+I as a linked disclosure-consent-controls cluster**. The strongest evidence is that the committee itself previously tagged these as the “red-zone” blockers and “must-fix” items for 1:1 follow-up: **assessment validity posture, detector posture, notice/consent/opt-out, human-centered learning, teacher-owned feedback, plus the unresolved definition locks on high-stakes work, AI assistance, and risk-based limits**.

heading_path: 1) WS-POL-E — Staff and Teacher Use of AI
sections.text:
This is plainly still live.

The committee’s own decision-ready rewrite treated **teacher-owned feedback** as a red-zone unresolved item with two materially different options:

* “**Educators may use AI to assist drafting feedback; educators must review, personalize, and own final feedback** …” versus
* “**Do not allow AI to generate evaluative feedback**; AI may assist only with non-evaluative supports …”

The survey record shows a real split, not just wording variation.

**David Berol** (survey response completed **2026-02-24**) wrote:
“**To maintain the student-teacher relationship, FCCPS staff may not use Generative AI at any stage of the preparation of student feedback or student evaluation materials.**” He then added: “**Any teacher automation of feedback is completely unacceptable.**”

By contrast, other members supported a guarded drafting posture. In the survey:

heading_path: 1) WS-POL-E — Staff and Teacher Use of AI
sections.text:
* **Elizabeth Chua** chose: “**Allow AI-assisted drafting; teacher reviews/personalizes; AI cannot be sole source of evaluative feedback.**” 
* **Adriana Palacios** supported substantially the same line, emphasizing that AI may assist drafting but human judgment and personalization must remain central. 
* **Jillian Burkley** likewise supported AI-assisted drafting with teacher responsibility retained. 
* **Susan** also selected the same general posture in the survey results.

The earlier drafting record also shows **David’s Meeting 6 contributions** taking a harder line: “**assessment and evaluative feedback that purports to be from the teacher should not (in general) incorporate substantive GenAI content**,” with only narrow exceptions such as review, disclosure, and prior parental consent.

**Practical takeaway:** WS-POL-E should stay on the triage list. The real unresolved question is **where the line falls between prohibited evaluative use and allowable formative/drafting support**, plus whether parent consent/disclosure remains part of that line. The record supports a real policy difference here, not just editing noise.

This should also be treated as a top-tier live issue.

You already have contemporaneous evidence from **Tina Beaty’s email of 2026-04-24** that “**some committee members share her concern and support a ‘restriction-first posture for younger students,’ even if that position is not reflected in the final committee recommendations due to the group editing process.**”

That is reinforced by the community input from **Sara Debus-Sherrill** on **2026-04-20**, who explicitly asked the committee to “**PLEASE consider a full ban for use with elementary school students**.”

The survey record shows that this is not only a public comment issue; it also tracks real committee variation.

**David Berol** (2026-02-24) wrote on the non-AI path item:
“**Option A: Guarantee a non-AI path wherever AI is optional; no penalty for opting out.**” He added: “**Students are better off using zero GenAI … we certainly should support 100% those students who want no GenAI in their schooling.**”

**Tina Beaty** pushed a similarly stronger developmental posture in her survey comments, warning that a design-first or permissive framing may not provide “**younger students the protection that they need in terms of exposure, usage, and direct contact with AI.**” She also raised K–5 developmental and exposure-risk concerns in her long-form comments.

By contrast, several members supported a **grade-banded normalization** approach rather than a younger-student restriction-first default:

* **Elizabeth Chua** supported “**Grade-banded approach: non-AI path guaranteed where AI is optional; AI expectations increase with age/skill, with supports and alternatives.**” 
* **Adriana Palacios** supported the same overall architecture. 
* **Jillian Burkley** likewise supported the grade-banded progression model.

The prior drafting material also shows a strong substantive distinction between the two sub-sections:

* **WS-POL-F** draft language for PreK–5 says GenAI use “**should be primarily oriented towards teaching AI Literacy**” and “**used minimally**” for applied uses, with close adult supervision. 
* **WS-POL-G** draft language for grades 6–12 says it is “**appropriate to expect that students will start using GenAI tools**,” but with pragmatic restrictions to avoid dependency.

**Practical takeaway:** F+G is not just a style issue. The live question is whether the final narrative has **under-described the younger-student restriction camp** and whether it has **overstated convergence** on grade-banded normalization. Tina’s 2026-04-24 email is especially important because it directly alleges underrepresentation in the current edited package.

heading_path: 3) WS-POL-L — Public Accountability, Notice, Consent, and Feedback
sections.text:
Even with Tom’s sentence completed, this section is still likely to consume time unless you frame it tightly.

The committee’s own “Part 2” rewrite marked **notice / consent / opt-out** as a red-zone unresolved issue with three different directions:

* advance notice plus consent/opt-out where feasible,
* consent/opt-out for any student-data use,
* notice-only with strong minimization/tool controls.

The named survey responses show real divergence:

**David Berol** (2026-02-24) criticized the original notice/consent formulation as operationally unworkable and overbroad, especially if it tries to cover all AI on campus rather than a tighter GenAI scope. He wrote that the “**where feasible proviso is an absolute magnet for controversy**” and that broad opt-in/opt-out collection would be an “**implementation nightmare**.”

**Tina Beaty** took the opposite direction and proposed stronger safeguards, including:
“**FCCPS will provide advance notice of approved and restricted AI uses and data practices, and will offer consent/opt-out options where feasible. FCCPS will prohibit model training on student data unless otherwise noted with parental consent.**”

heading_path: 3) WS-POL-L — Public Accountability, Notice, Consent, and Feedback
sections.text:
**Anubav Vasudevan** also expressed feasibility concerns, worrying that opt-out could require “**two parallel curricula**,” which he said “**doesn’t seem feasible**.”

**Elizabeth Chua**, **Adriana Palacios**, and **Jillian Burkley** all supported variants of the middle position: notice for all, consent/opt-out where feasible, with data minimization and approved tools as defaults.

**Practical takeaway:** L is still live, but it is narrower than E and F+G. The real question is not whether transparency matters; the split is over **how broad the consent/opt-out right is, how operationally feasible it is, and whether the scope should be narrowed to GenAI / student-data uses rather than “all AI.”**

heading_path: 4) WS-POL-H+I — Student Use Categories, Controls, Disclosure, and Process Evidence
sections.text:
I would keep this as the next tier, especially if today’s straw poll surfaces disclosure or detectors.

The committee’s own blocker list put all of these in the unresolved zone:

* **R2 Assessment validity posture**
* **R3 Detector posture**
* **D1 High-stakes definition**
* **D2 AI assistance scope definition**
* **D3 Risk-based rubric**

That matters because even where people appear to agree on a principle, they often disagree on what the terms mean.

For example, the survey record shows that **David Berol** did not merely prefer stronger detector guardrails; he argued for **no detectors in integrity decisions**, calling detector use “**fruit of the poison tree**” and saying “**AI detectors have zero place in FCCPS**” absent far more exacting review.

By contrast:

* **Elizabeth Chua** supported “**Detector outputs are advisory only and require local validation; never sole evidence in decisions.**” 
* **Adriana Palacios** supported the same advisory-only posture. 
* **Jillian Burkley** supported the same advisory-only posture. 
* **Susan** and **Tina** also supported the advisory-only framing in the survey.

heading_path: 4) WS-POL-H+I — Student Use Categories, Controls, Disclosure, and Process Evidence
sections.text:
Disclosure is similarly not settled just because most people support “disclosure.” The record shows disagreement over **how broad disclosure should be** and whether “high-stakes” is the right anchor:

* **David Berol** said the options were too blunt and that disclosure depends on grade, subject, exact use, and assessment context. 
* **Elizabeth Chua** favored grade-banded guidance with teacher flexibility. 
* **Tina Beaty** wanted disclosure for any AI use in student work, not only high-stakes contexts.

**Practical takeaway:** H+I is probably the most likely place for **false consensus caused by unresolved definitions**. If current section language treats detector posture or disclosure posture as broadly settled, that is overstated. If the current narrative already preserves the split cleanly, it may not need much meeting time.

heading_path: 5) WS-POL-B and WS-POL-D — only if the discussion starts collapsing into undefined terms
sections.text:
These are not my first use of meeting time, but they are the **cross-cutting hidden blockers**.

The governance record shows the committee explicitly created **definition locks** for:

* “**High-stakes work**”
* what counts as “**AI assistance**”
* the plain-language meaning of “**risk-based**” limits.

And Tina’s 2026-04-24 email suggests a possible under-characterization in the overall posture section: the record may contain more support for a **restriction-first posture for younger students** than the current recommendations reflect.

So B/D are best treated as **enablers**: if E, F+G, or H+I get stuck on “high-stakes,” “AI assistance,” “risk-based,” or overall posture, then pull the discussion up to B or D.

1. **WS-POL-E**
2. **WS-POL-F+G**
3. **WS-POL-L and/or WS-POL-H+I** as one linked cluster
4. **WS-POL-B / D** only if definitional ambiguity is what is blocking agreement

I would not say the record proves broad committee backing for Sara’s exact position. What the record supports is narrower: **there is documented parent concern**, **Tina believes some committee members share that younger-student restriction posture**, and the final edited package may not fully reflect that breadth. That is enough to justify putting **F+G** on the live triage list, but not enough to characterize it as a formal committee majority position.

If you want, I can turn this into a **2-minute chair triage script** for the opening of Meeting 7.
